inputPapers.title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation
inputPapers.abstract: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.

inputPapers.title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
inputPapers.abstract: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

inputPapers.title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
inputPapers.abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.

inputPapers.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
inputPapers.abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

inputPapers.title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
inputPapers.abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

inputPapers.title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
inputPapers.abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

inputPapers.title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
inputPapers.abstract: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.

inputPapers.title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
inputPapers.abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm.

inputPapers.title: Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: Mitigating Rubric Hacking through Latent Dimension Recovery and Balancing
inputPapers.abstract: Rubric hacking limits both performance and training robustness in rubric-based reinforcement learning. By decomposing rubrics into sub-dimensions, we reveal the Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: as the total rubric score increases, certain sub-dimension scores systematically decrease, suggesting the model sacrifices specific quality aspects to optimize the aggregated objective. From the sub-dimension perspective, we observe two phenomena: (1) dimension imbalance, causing the policy to favor heavily covered dimensions; (2) dimension absence, leading to a systematic gap between rewards and true quality. To mitigate these issues, we propose Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA), which has generations compete within each dimension separately to mitigate rubric imbalance, and Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC), which mines evaluation dimensions implicitly encoded in a holistic preference signal to complete rubric coverage. Experiments in chat, science, and medical domains indicate that FRDA mitigates rubric hacking with more stable improvements, while RSDC outperforms both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation, yielding generally higher-quality responses.

inputPapers.title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
inputPapers.abstract: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

inputPapers.title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization
inputPapers.abstract: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.

inputPapers.title: Nested Shared-Operator Recursion on ARC-AGI-1: An Empirical Study of HRM, TRM and URM
inputPapers.abstract: Recursive reasoning models refine persistent internal states by repeatedly applying learned operators. We investigate whether adding a persistent intermediate state that integrates repeated updates of a faster state through the same operator improves predictive performance relative to each model family's baseline at matched parameter counts. We define this organisation operationally and implement it within three architectures: the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) and Universal Reasoning Model (URM). Using the official codebases on ARC-AGI-1, we compare each baseline with its parameter-matched nested variant. We evaluate held-out queries from tasks whose demonstrations were available during training. The experiments use a single-GPU budget far below the published training protocols. Under the tested conditions, nested variants show no consistent advantage in token accuracy, predictive loss or exact solving, which remains near zero for all configurations. The results therefore leave the hypothesis open. We specify a confirmatory comparison, with an informative baseline, multiple seeds, controls that isolate nesting and predefined criteria, to determine whether this organisation merits further development.

inputPapers.title: The Development of Sycophancy in Language Models: Tracing Vulnerabilities from Pretraining to Post-Training
inputPapers.abstract: Language models can change a committed answer to accommodate a user's opinion or pushback without new evidence. However, when this behaviour develops during training and what a released model inherits from earlier stages remain unclear. We follow 741 checkpoints of 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to released models. We plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far a model follows a user's stated opinion or abandons its verdict under pressure. In most lineages the behaviour is present before post-training, and its average strength changes in either direction, at different stages across lineages. A clearer pattern emerges at the level of individual questions. Beyond responses without pressure, pretraining behaviour predicts little of which questions a released model yields on. That pattern forms during post-training: on routes with supervised fine-tuning, the fine-tuning checkpoint predicts part of it and the preference-optimization checkpoint most of it. A sibling trained from the same base along another route predicts far less: for Tülu-3 8B, its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, a sibling 19%. Internal states add predictive information without changing this ranking. Similar average scores conceal different vulnerabilities, and training history matters for auditing a released model.

inputPapers.title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
inputPapers.abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

inputPapers.title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed
inputPapers.abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.

inputPapers.title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation
inputPapers.abstract: Long-horizon tasks are important for modern AI and robotics, yet pose a challenge for reinforcement learning. Historically, a popular approach has been to decompose a task into subgoals, and learn a subgoal-conditioned policy to execute each subtask in sequence. We introduce an alternative called Value Disaggregation (VaDar), which trains a single subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values. Because subgoal information is needed only at training-time, VaDar removes the need for possibly costly or cumbersome subgoal-selection during policy deployment. Moreover, through careful experiments, we show that VaDar (1) is always competitive with, and frequently outperforms, natural baselines like goal-conditioning and (2) succeeds on tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple optimization objectives. In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the RoboCasa suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar's successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning, whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.

inputPapers.title: SleepPairNet: Learning Multimodal Pediatric Sleep Representations with Random-Pair Cross-Attention
inputPapers.abstract: Analyzing physiological sleep signals is important for assessing sleep quality and detecting sleep-related disorders. Learning inter-modal relationships across physiological signals can provide richer representations for downstream sleep analysis. We introduce \textbf{SleepPairNet}, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns pairwise interactions between physiological signals through cross-attention. We propose a random modality-pair selection strategy that exposes the model to diverse signal pairs during pretraining, enabling flexibility across modality combinations at test time. Pretrained on the NCH dataset, SleepPairNet outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks while remaining competitive on EEG-related tasks, and shows even stronger results when transferred to the external CHAT dataset.

inputPapers.title: Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC): A Mechanism for Time-Aware Pediatric Sleep Representation Learning
inputPapers.abstract: Sleep physiology evolves throughout the night, with changes in sleep cycles, respiratory stability, and cardiovascular dynamics. However, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep typically process short, fixed-duration windows without explicitly modeling where each window occurs within the full sleep session. We introduce Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC), a mechanism that complements local positional encodings by conditioning latent representations on the global time-of-sleep of each input window. We integrate GTC into three representative SSL frameworks and evaluate them on five clinically relevant tasks with extreme class imbalance across two independent pediatric cohorts. GTC generally improves F1 and AUPRC across architectures and tasks, with gains persisting under cross-cohort transfer, highlighting the value of global temporal context for sleep representation learning.

inputPapers.title: Degree Bounds for Separating Polynomial and Neural Invariants for Point Clouds
inputPapers.abstract: Neural networks that respect the symmetries of point clouds commonly compute high-order representations of the rotation group to improve their expressivity. Such models are known to be universal, and thus able to separate any pair of point clouds, when using representations of sufficiently high order, yet no precise bound on this order, as a function of the number of points, was previously known. We establish the first quadratic lower and upper degree bounds for polynomials that separate point clouds of n points up to rotations and permutations. By showing Tensor Field Networks and MACE can express all invariant polynomials of a given degree with sufficient representation order, we additionally derive the first explicit, quadratic bound on the representation order sufficient for these architectures to be complete, replacing previous existence results with concrete guarantees. We further show that, under local regularity assumptions, point cloud separation can be achieved with a message-passing-based model using invariants whose degree depends only on the size of a local neighborhood, rather than on the size of the full point cloud. Finally, we provide counterexamples showing MACE must compute high order irreducible representations to separate locally regular point clouds.

inputPapers.title: A Probabilistic, Rotation-Preserving Kernel Operator Surrogate for Continuum-Robot Design Spaces
inputPapers.abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware, operator-learning-based surrogate for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) that generalizes across robot design and actuation while predicting the complete equilibrium configuration. Our central idea is a nonstationary Gaussian-process (GP) kernel whose metric is learned by a shallow neural network from mechanics-aware design coordinates. The network learns how similarity changes across design space, while the resulting kernel defines the design-to-pose operator, its posterior uncertainty, and a criterion for sequential simulator acquisition. We represent backbone position and rotational strain with spatial kernels and reconstruct orientation directly on SO(3), preserving valid material frames and tendon geometry. We use ASkotch with Nystrom preconditioning for scalable kernel operator solves and a separate Nystrom approximation for posterior covariance. Experiments show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean trajectory error by approximately 15% relative to IID sampling, while posterior variance increases for increasingly unsupported designs. Compared with prior neural-operator TDCR models, the method is 30-50% more accurate using approximately 5x fewer training designs while additionally providing posterior uncertainty estimates.

inputPapers.title: ITU-DESC: a missingness-aware machine-learning dementia risk score in the UK Biobank cohort
inputPapers.abstract: Background: Existing dementia risk scores rely on fixed, pre-selected features and linear models, or ignore bias from informative missingness in cohort data. Here we introduce the Istanbul Technical University Dementia Risk Score (ITU-DESC), an explainable machine-learning score for incident all-cause dementia that combines broad feature selection across roughly 8,000 candidate features with explicit control of missingness bias. Results: We studied approximately 500,000 UK Biobank participants with a median follow-up of 16.6 years. We withheld missingness patterns from the model using unconditional random hot-deck imputation. We stabilized feature selection by repeating BorutaSHAP-based feature selection with ten random-imputation seeds and selecting predictors chosen in at least eight of the ten seeds, which yielded 38 predictors. We trained a CatBoost gradient-boosted decision-tree model and evaluated it on a holdout test set of 50,041 participants. For all-cause incident dementia, ITU-DESC achieved an average precision of 0.138 (95% confidence interval 0.123-0.156) and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.853 (0.844-0.863), significantly outperforming other risk scores, including the strongest comparator, the UK Biobank Dementia Risk Prediction model (0.118 and 0.841). We identified dementia risk predictors absent from established scores, including leukocyte telomere length and liver enzymes. Conclusions: ITU-DESC is the first dementia risk score to combine broad feature selection with explicit control of missingness bias.

inputPapers.title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
inputPapers.abstract: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

inputPapers.title: Concerns in Benchmarking Jailbreaks: An Empirical Study of Attack Success Rates
inputPapers.abstract: Jailbreak methods are commonly compared using Attack Success Rate (ASR), but these comparisons depend on how responses are generated and judged. In this paper, we examine eight attacks against three open-weight language models using three evaluation procedures. Low-resource language attacks achieve a mean ASR of 96.0% under keyword matching but 2.7% under a Qwen3 evaluator following StrongREJECT scoring instructions. Changing the number and arrangement of attempts reverses the ranking of DeepInception and rewriting. In a separate experiment, sampling 100 responses for each unchanged request at Ollama's default temperature of 0.8 yields 100% ASR under keyword matching but 50% under the Qwen3 evaluator. Beyond evaluator sensitivity, these findings raise a safety concern: repeated sampling can expose residual unsafe behavior despite an initial refusal, suggesting probabilistic suppression rather than robust exclusion. We recommend explicit success definitions, matched response budgets, validated evaluators, and reporting cumulative failure under repeated interaction rather than relying on single-generation tests.

inputPapers.title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting
inputPapers.abstract: Recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) can consume covariates in-context, extending zero-shot forecasting to problems driven by external factors. This enables scenario analysis: forecasting how a target responds to events that set covariates to chosen future values. Whether they can do this reliably is an open question. We introduce WhatIf-Bench, a benchmark measuring how well forecasters use covariates to forecast a target's response to future events. WhatIf-Bench is semi-synthetic: time series come from mechanistic simulators of data centers, power grids, road traffic, and water networks, with controlled covariate-target relationships grounded in each system. Each task presents a history of events intervening on covariates, then asks to forecast a future event that either replays seen values (Replay) or sets them to unseen ones (Novel). Skill on Novel futures also falls as events set more covariates jointly. More historical events raise skill on Novel futures across the board, but large differences remain. WhatIf-Bench reveals generalization to Novel futures as the core challenge, and offers a testbed toward arbitrary scenario analysis.

inputPapers.title: SafeWall: A Risk-Aware Job Walltime Recommendation for HPC Scheduling
inputPapers.abstract: In high-performance computing (HPC), users must submit resource requirements for their jobs, with user-supplied walltime being a critical parameter. The core of our approach is a risk-aware buffer that dynamically calibrates safety margins based on individual user's historical behavior. When user data is limited, the system employs statistical shrinkage to align these margins with a global baseline, ensuring robustness. This yields a lightweight mechanism that optimizes the trade-off between prediction accuracy and termination risk. SafeWall is modular and applicable to various learning-based prediction models. We evaluate SafeWall using five public workload traces, including the full-lifetime job log from the 4,392-node Theta machine at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Across all traces, SafeWall substantially reduces underestimation risk compared to the unbuffered base predictors, while preserving competitive accuracy. rawOutput.titleZh: 重复下的复制：从前缀匹配到位置哈希

summarySections.backgroundAndQuestion: 现代大语言模型虽能近乎完美地复制随机文本，但在处理长串重复字符时常出现提前终止或无限重复的错误。这是因为基于局部内容匹配的‘归纳头’机制在重复序列中无法区分不同位置，导致模型难以判断何时停止复制。论文聚焦于这一重复敏感性问题，探究浅层低精度模型能否在任意重复下正确完成复制与终止。
summarySections.modelAndSetup: 研究设定为在固定词汇表上，让同一模型参数复制任意长度不超过设计上限N的字符串，并正确结束。输入为源字符串加复制指令，输出需逐字还原并以结束符终止。评估采用合成数据，涵盖均匀随机、中度重复和全同字符三种分布，在训练长度内外测试精确复制率，重点观察模型对重复结构的泛化能力。
summarySections.contributionsAndResults: 论文证明一个两层、O(log log N)-比特精度、O(log N/log log N)宽度的Transformer可通过位置哈希机制可靠复制任意字符串并正确终止。实验显示，传统位置编码模型在长重复串上性能骤降，而基于值旋转（VO-RoPE）的模型在训练长度2000内达到完美复制，并外推至5005仍保持近完美准确率，验证了理论构造的有效性。
summarySections.methodsAndTechniques: 方法核心是用值/输出旋转（VO-RoPE）将位置编码为小素数周期的模余数，通过中国剩余定理联合解码唯一偏移量。第一层注意力锚定分隔符并写入相对距离的周期指纹，第二层利用该指纹检索下一个源标记或结束符。该机制不依赖内容匹配，而是通过位置哈希实现统一的检索规则，从而绕开重复带来的歧义。
summarySections.limitationsAndReadingValue: 理论下界仅适用于最终常数偏置类模型，实验中的VO模型依赖特定周期乘积，超出后因模冲突而失效，限制了其通用性。此外，模拟FP8精度与实际部署仍有差距。最值得阅读的是其将位置信息嵌入值通路的设计思想、理论与实验结合的严谨性，以及对当前LLM重复失败模式的形式化解释。

rawOutput.titleZh: 超越下层强凸性的牛顿型双层优化方法

summarySections.backgroundAndQuestion: 双层优化广泛用于超参数学习、数据加权等任务，但传统牛顿法依赖下层强凸性以确保唯一解和可逆Hessian。当下层解不唯一时，经典超梯度公式失效，现有方法需解平方Hessian系统，计算昂贵且不稳定。本文旨在突破这一限制，在下层非强凸甚至Hessian奇异时仍能高效求解。
summarySections.modelAndSetup: 论文研究一般双层问题，其中下层目标可能非强凸、解集多点，上层目标依赖其最优解。通过KKT条件重构原问题，采用残差最小化视角，输入为上下层函数及其导数，输出为近似稳定点。在合成问题、数据清洗与GPT-2重加权任务上测试，评估指标为各阶KKT残差下降速度与最终性能。
summarySections.contributionsAndResults: 提出两种新型牛顿法：Newton-based GALET在正谱隙条件下直接利用范围结构避免平方系统；Newton-based BAMM借助强凸聚合模型耦合更新。两者均获理论收敛保证，并在复杂度上优于基线。实验显示其更快降低残差，尤其在病态条件下更稳健，验证了共享曲率结构的有效性。
summarySections.methodsAndTechniques: 核心思想是利用下层与乘子更新间的共享曲率结构。GALET利用Hessian值域包含梯度的性质，用同一线性系统同时逼近下层解与乘子；BAMM则构造随迭代衰减的强凸聚合函数，使Hessian始终可逆。二者均采用不精确牛顿步，通过梯度下降求解线性系统，避免显式矩阵求逆。
summarySections.limitationsAndReadingValue: 方法依赖Hessian-向量积，对大规模模型内存开销大，且假设条件如谱隙或凸性未必总成立。实验虽涵盖神经网络，但未在更大模型上验证扩展性。最值得读的是其统一框架GNBO，清晰揭示了多类双层算法的共性结构，对设计高效二阶方法具指导意义。

rawOutput.titleZh: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps

summarySections.backgroundAndQuestion: 现有基于直接策略优化的深度学习方法在求解高维连续时间随机控制问题时，因需通过整个时间离散化动态进行反向传播，常面临梯度消失/爆炸、误差累积和训练不稳定等问题。尤其当系统包含跳跃扩散过程时，传统方法更难处理。本文旨在克服这些数值挑战，提供一种更稳定高效的替代方案。
summarySections.modelAndSetup: 研究设定为带跳跃扩散的连续时间随机控制问题，目标是最大化期望奖励。状态轨迹由含布朗运动和泊松随机测度的SDE驱动，控制为马尔可夫反馈形式。模型采用神经网络分别逼近控制策略和伴随变量，通过模拟轨迹生成数据，并以终端奖励和运行奖励定义目标函数，评估指标为策略性能与最优解的接近程度。
summarySections.contributionsAndResults: 提出了一种名为Deep PMP的新框架，其核心贡献在于分离伴随学习与策略更新。该方法不仅避免了端到端反向传播的稳定性问题，还能自然处理跳跃项。数值实验在多个高维非线性基准上验证了其优于直接策略优化的精度与稳定性，结果可信且具说服力。
summarySections.methodsAndTechniques: 方法基于Pontryagin最大值原理，首先固定当前控制策略，沿模拟轨迹使用反向传播计算路径伴随标签，再通过监督回归将其投影为马尔可夫伴随场。随后利用该场通过逐点哈密顿驻留条件更新控制策略。关键技术在于将伴随变量的学习转化为回归问题，从而解耦长期依赖。
summarySections.limitationsAndReadingValue: 局限在于收敛性分析仅针对理想投影伴随过程，未涵盖神经网络近似与优化误差；且未测试状态或控制依赖的跳跃强度情形。最值得阅读的是其方法设计与理论分析部分，展示了如何将经典最优控制理论与深度学习结合，为高维随机控制提供了新思路。

paper.title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding

rawOutput.titleZh: 通过变分解码实现并行语言模型

summarySections.backgroundAndQuestion: 传统自回归语言模型逐个生成token，导致推理延迟高，尤其在大模型上更严重。尽管推测解码和离散扩散等方法尝试提速，但前者受限于草稿模型质量，后者需多步迭代。本文旨在构建一种从单一定训练目标出发、能直接从序列数据学习并行生成的语言模型框架，在保持生成质量的同时显著提升推理速度。
summarySections.modelAndSetup: 模型采用共享权重的编码器-解码器结构，编码器为标准自回归模型，解码器通过辅助隐变量并行生成多个token。训练基于变分下界，结合自回归损失与并行重建损失。在预训练阶段使用通用语料，在后训练阶段加入指令微调与偏好优化。评估涵盖文本质量（负对数似然）、生成速度（tokens/s）及下游任务性能（如数学、编程）。
summarySections.contributionsAndResults: 提出并实现了完整的并行语言模型（PLM）训练方案，无需依赖教师模型蒸馏。实验证明，PLM在预训练阶段即可达到接近自回归模型的质量，并随模型规模增大而提升并行度。后训练后的1.3B和3B模型在数学、代码和指令遵循任务上表现相当或更优，同时推理速度快2.3至5.7倍，验证了高质量并行生成的可行性。
summarySections.methodsAndTechniques: 核心是通过隐变量协调并行预测：编码器将历史token映射为隐变量分布，解码器据此一次性生成多个未来token。训练目标由自回归损失与KL散度项构成，确保隐变量承载必要上下文信息。引入几何感知的Voronoi辅助空间和表示对齐损失，提升了训练效率与重建能力。推理时采用二次解码，结合宽松验证规则进一步提高吞吐量。
summarySections.limitationsAndReadingValue: 模型仍需验证步骤来保障生成一致性，完全单步无损生成尚未实现。训练计算开销高于纯自回归模型，且当前结果集中于特定规模。然而，其端到端训练范式、清晰的变分动机与可扩展性分析极具启发性。最值得阅读的是其统一的建模范式、高效的训练机制设计及系统的实验验证路径。

paper.title: Degree Bounds for Separating Polynomial and Neural Invariants for Point Clouds

rawOutput.titleZh: 点云分离多项式与神经不变量的度界

summarySections.backgroundAndQuestion: 为什么现有基于对称性的点云模型虽通用却缺乏定量保障？当前高阶张量网络如TFN和MACE被证明能分离任意非对称点云，但其完备性依赖于‘足够高’的表示阶数，具体需要多高始终未知。这导致实际设计中阶数选择依赖经验，无法平衡表达力与计算成本，尤其在局部消息传递架构下更不清楚邻域大小如何影响所需复杂度。
summarySections.modelAndSetup: 论文研究了在旋转与置换群作用下，多项式不变量分离点云所需的最小度数。输入是n个d维点构成的点云，输出是能区分不同轨道的不变函数。通过分析Gram矩阵的Sn轨道分离问题，并结合局部正则性假设，作者建立了分离度的上下界，并将其映射到TFN和MACE等模型的表示阶数需求，实验设定聚焦于理论边界推导而非具体数据集训练。
summarySections.contributionsAndResults: 论文首次给出了点云分离的二次下界与dn²量级上界，填补了不变量理论在此问题上的空白。由此导出TFN和MACE实现完备性所需表示阶数的首个显式二次界，取代了以往存在性结论。进一步，在局部正则假设下，分离仅依赖邻域大小的平方，但反例也表明高阶不可约表示不可或缺，为模型设计提供了精确指导。
summarySections.methodsAndTechniques: 作者利用中心化技巧将含平移的群作用转化为无平移情形，通过构造共面旋转多边形族证明下界，借助Gram矩阵与Sn轨道关系建立上界。关键在于将分离问题转化为低秩对称矩阵的轨道区分，并用拉格朗日插值与幂和多项式构造显式分离不变量。对于神经网络，则通过证明其可表达特定度数多项式来传递界限。
summarySections.limitationsAndReadingValue: 论文核心结论基于理想化假设，如局部强正则性和全局消息传递，实际中可能不成立。反例构造依赖特殊对称配置，现实点云未必触发。此外，未考虑非多项式激活的影响，下界是否紧仍开放。最值得读的是问题形式化过程、度界证明思路及对MACE超参的量化分析，为理解几何模型表达力提供了坚实理论基底。
